position: end — after the verb and its object; before participles (*humanely raised*)
contrast: *humanely* = kindly, without cruelty (гуманно); *humanly* = within human power, almost always in *humanly possible* (в человеческих силах).

senses.gloss: In a kind way that avoids causing pain or suffering.
examples: The shelter promises to treat every animal *humanely*.
Prisoners must be treated *humanely*, whatever their crimes.
The store sells eggs from *humanely* raised chickens.

position: before its word — almost always before *possible*
contrast: *humanely* = kindly, without cruelty (гуманно); *humanly* = within human power, almost always in *humanly possible* (в человеческих силах).

senses.gloss: Within what a person is able to do.
examples: We'll get there as fast as *humanly* possible.
It's not *humanly* possible to read all those files by Monday.
The doctors did everything *humanly* possible to save him.

position: mid or end — mid before verbs of speaking (*I humbly apologize*), end otherwise

senses.gloss: In a modest way, without pride.
examples: I *humbly* apologize for the mistake.
She accepted the award *humbly*, thanking her whole team.
He *humbly* admitted that he had been wrong.

position: end — after the verb; before its word with adjectives (*humiliatingly slow*)

senses.gloss: In a way that makes someone feel ashamed and foolish.
examples: The team lost *humiliatingly*, 10 to 0, at home.
He was *humiliatingly* slow on the obstacle course.
Her request was *humiliatingly* turned down in front of everyone.

position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it

senses.gloss: In a funny or amusing way.
examples: He described the disastrous trip *humorously*.
The speech was *humorously* written but made a serious point.
She *humorously* called her tiny apartment “the palace.”

position: end — after the verb, usually as *a hundredfold*

senses.gloss: By a hundred times; enormously.
examples: The price of the land has increased a *hundredfold*.
Their investment was repaid a *hundredfold*.
Computing power has grown more than a *hundredfold* since then.

position: end — after the verb and its object

senses.gloss: In an eager way, like someone who is hungry.
examples: The kids ate *hungrily* after the game.
The dog watched *hungrily* as I cut the steak.
She read every book on the subject *hungrily*.

position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it

senses.gloss: Quickly, because there is not much time.
examples: He *hurriedly* packed a bag and left.
The report was written *hurriedly* and full of errors.
We said goodbye *hurriedly* and ran for the train.

position: end — usually after a verb of speaking or looking

senses.gloss: In a low, rough voice.
examples: “Thank you,” she said *huskily*.
He laughed *huskily*, still hoarse from his cold.
The singer whispered the last line *huskily* into the mic.

position: end — after the verb and its object; before participles (*hygienically sealed*)

senses.gloss: In a clean way that prevents disease.
examples: Food must be stored and handled *hygienically*.
The instruments are *hygienically* sealed after cleaning.
Is there a way to share a water bottle *hygienically*?

position: end — after the verb; front in *speaking hyperbolically*

senses.gloss: With deliberate exaggeration, not meant literally.
examples: Speaking *hyperbolically*, he called it the worst day in human history.
Critics *hyperbolically* described the film as the greatest ever made.
She wasn't being literal; she was talking *hyperbolically*.

position: end — after the verb; before its word with adjectives (*hypnotically beautiful*)

senses.gloss: In a way that holds your attention, as if you were hypnotized.
examples: The lights on the water flickered *hypnotically*.
The song's beat is *hypnotically* repetitive.
The snake swayed *hypnotically* in front of the crowd.

position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it

senses.gloss: In a way that criticizes others for what you do yourself.
examples: He *hypocritically* complained about noise while playing drums at midnight.
Critics said the company was acting *hypocritically* by praising clean energy while drilling for oil.
She lectured us *hypocritically* about being late, then showed up an hour late herself.

position: front — often with a comma; also mid

senses.gloss: As an imagined situation, not a real one.
examples: *Hypothetically*, what would you do with a million dollars?
Let's say, *hypothetically*, that the flight gets canceled.
The drug could *hypothetically* help millions of patients.

position: end — after the verb in the manner sense; before its word in the degree sense (*hysterically funny*)

senses.gloss: In a wildly emotional, uncontrolled way.
examples: The baby cried *hysterically* until her mother came back.
He was laughing *hysterically* and couldn't stop.

senses.gloss: Extremely, used almost only with *funny*.
examples: The movie was *hysterically* funny.
Her stories about her kids are *hysterically* funny.

position: front — of the words it explains, after a comma or inside parentheses
modifies: a phrase or clause that restates or narrows what came before
form: abbreviation of Latin *id est* 'that is'; read aloud as *that is* or letter by letter
contrast: *i.e.* restates or narrows (= *that is*, то есть); *e.g.* gives examples (= *for example*, например). *Bring something warm, e.g., a sweater* leaves other options; *Bring your warmest item, i.e., the sweater* does not. American style puts a comma after both.

senses.gloss: That is; in other words.
examples: The course is for beginners, *i.e.*, people with no programming experience.
Submit the form by the deadline (*i.e.*, Friday at 5 p.m.).
We need a bigger budget, *i.e.*, more money from the city.

position: end — usually after a verb of speaking or looking

senses.gloss: In a very unfriendly, cold way.
examples: “I don't think so,” she said *icily*.
He stared *icily* at the reporter and walked away.
The proposal was received *icily* by the board.

position: end — after the verb and its object; before participles (*identically dressed*)

senses.gloss: In exactly the same way.
examples: The twins were dressed *identically* for the photo.
Both machines performed *identically* in the test.
The two contracts are worded almost *identically*.

type: viewpoint — from the point of view of ideology
position: before its word — before adjectives and participles (*ideologically opposed*); also front

senses.gloss: In terms of political or social beliefs.
examples: The two parties are *ideologically* opposed on almost every issue.
*Ideologically*, the new mayor is hard to pin down.
The group is *ideologically* driven rather than profit-driven.

position: end — after the verb and its object
modifies: verbs of speaking, writing and translating

senses.gloss: In the natural way that native speakers use a language.
examples: Her English is fluent, but she doesn't always speak *idiomatically*.
Try to translate the sentence *idiomatically*, not word for word.
A native speaker would say it *more idiomatically*.

position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it; *stand idly by* is fixed

senses.gloss: Without doing anything useful, or without any real purpose.
examples: We can't just stand *idly* by while the park is destroyed.
He sat *idly* flipping through channels all afternoon.
I *idly* wondered what my old classmates were doing now.

position: before its word — before participles and adjectives (*idyllically located*); also end

senses.gloss: In a peaceful, beautiful way, like a perfect picture.
examples: The cabin is *idyllically* located on a quiet lake.
They spent the summer *idyllically* in a small Vermont town.
The village looked *idyllically* peaceful under the snow.

position: end — after verbs like *end*, *lose*, *fail*; also before participles

senses.gloss: In a way that brings public shame.
examples: The campaign ended *ignominiously* after just three weeks.
The champion was *ignominiously* knocked out in the first round.
He was *ignominiously* fired in front of his whole team.

position: end — in *speak ill of*, *think ill of*; mid in *can ill afford*; before participles in compounds
comparison: not gradable — its old forms *worse*, *worst* are now felt as the forms of *badly*
form: flat — the same form as the adjective *ill*
contrast: *ill* meaning sick (*She's ill*, *He felt ill*) is the adjective, not this adverb, and American speech usually says *sick* there. Before a participle the adverb makes a hyphenated adjective: *an ill-advised plan*, *ill-fitting shoes*.

senses.gloss: Badly or unkindly; in an unfavorable way.
examples: Don't speak *ill* of the dead.
I don't think *ill* of him for leaving.
The team was *ill*-prepared for the cold weather.

senses.gloss: Hardly; only with difficulty, in *can ill afford*.
examples: We can *ill* afford another delay.
It's a mistake the company can *ill* afford right now.

position: end — after the verb and its object; before participles (*illegally parked*)

senses.gloss: In a way that is against the law.
examples: My car was towed because it was *illegally* parked.
He was fined for downloading movies *illegally*.
The factory had been dumping waste *illegally* for years.

position: end — after the verb and its object

senses.gloss: In a way that is too messy to read.
examples: The doctor wrote the prescription so *illegibly* that the pharmacist called him.
Her name was scrawled *illegibly* at the bottom of the page.
He writes *more illegibly* than anyone I know.

position: end — after the verb and its object; before participles

senses.gloss: Without a legal or fair right.
examples: The court ruled that the land had been taken *illegitimately*.
Critics claimed the election had been won *illegitimately*.
The funds were *illegitimately* moved to a private account.

position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it

senses.gloss: In a way that is forbidden by law or by rules.
examples: The drugs were *illicitly* smuggled across the border.
He was accused of *illicitly* recording the meeting.
The paintings had been sold *illicitly* to collectors abroad.

position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it; also front with a comma

senses.gloss: In a way that does not follow reason.
examples: People often behave *illogically* when they're scared.
She argued, a little *illogically*, that the plan was both too cheap and too expensive.
*Illogically*, I felt guilty even though it wasn't my fault.

position: end — after the verb and its object

senses.gloss: In a creative, original way.
examples: The old warehouse has been *imaginatively* turned into apartments.
The teacher uses games *imaginatively* to explain math.
The movie tells the story *more imaginatively* than the book does.

position: before its word — before participles and adjectives (*immaculately dressed*); also end

senses.gloss: Perfectly, especially perfectly clean or neat.
examples: He always arrives *immaculately* dressed.
The house was *immaculately* clean when we moved in.
The garden is kept *immaculately* all year round.

position: end — after the verb and its object

senses.gloss: In a childish way, not as an adult should.
examples: He reacted *immaturely* and slammed the door.
Stop acting so *immaturely*; you're thirty years old.
Both candidates behaved *immaturely* during the debate.

position: before its word — before adjectives and comparatives (*immeasurably better*); also end

senses.gloss: Very much; to a degree too great to measure.
examples: Her new job is *immeasurably* better than the old one.
The program has helped the community *immeasurably*.
Losing his father affected him *immeasurably*.

position: end — after the verb; also before its word (*imminently dangerous*)
contrast: *imminently* (вот-вот) is easy to confuse with *eminently* (весьма, в высшей степени): *an eminently reasonable idea*, *eminently qualified*.

senses.gloss: Very soon; about to happen.
examples: An announcement is expected *imminently*.
The building was declared *imminently* dangerous and closed.
The two companies are *imminently* expected to sign the deal.

position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it

senses.gloss: In a way that is morally wrong.
examples: The company acted *immorally*, but not illegally.
Many voters felt the senator had behaved *immorally*.
They profited *immorally* from other people's suffering.

position: end — after the verb and its object

senses.gloss: Fairly, without favoring any side.
examples: A judge must listen to both sides *impartially*.
The report presents the facts *impartially*.
The prize money was divided *impartially* among the finalists.

position: end — usually after a verb of speaking or looking

senses.gloss: Without showing any emotion.
examples: The guard watched us *impassively* from the gate.
She listened *impassively* as the verdict was read.
He stared *impassively* at the screen.

position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it

senses.gloss: In a way that shows you don't want to wait.
examples: He tapped his foot *impatiently* while he waited.
The kids are *impatiently* waiting for summer vacation.
“Come on, hurry up,” she said *impatiently*.

position: before its word — before participles and adjectives (*impeccably dressed*); also end

senses.gloss: Perfectly, with no faults at all.
examples: The waiter was *impeccably* dressed in a black suit.
The choir performed *impeccably* last night.
Her manners are *impeccably* polite.

position: end — after the verb; also mid

senses.gloss: So slightly or slowly that it can hardly be noticed.
examples: The light changed *imperceptibly* as the sun went down.
She nodded almost *imperceptibly*.
Prices have been rising slowly, almost *imperceptibly*, all year.

position: end — after the verb and its object; before participles

senses.gloss: Not completely or not correctly; with faults.
examples: The disease is still only *imperfectly* understood.
I speak Spanish, but *imperfectly*.
The old photos were *imperfectly* restored.

position: end — usually after a verb of speaking or looking

senses.gloss: In a proud, commanding way, expecting to be obeyed.
examples: She waved *imperiously* for the waiter.
“Bring me the file,” he said *imperiously*.
The cat stared *imperiously* at its empty bowl.

position: end — after the verb and its object

senses.gloss: Without personal feeling or warmth.
examples: The letter was written *impersonally*, as if by a machine.
Big hospitals can treat patients very *impersonally*.
He spoke *impersonally* about the layoffs, never mentioning names.

position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it

senses.gloss: Quickly and without thinking first.
examples: He *impetuously* quit his job and moved to Alaska.
She acted *impetuously* and regretted it later.
The young soldier charged *impetuously* ahead of the others.

position: end — usually after a verb of speaking or looking

senses.gloss: In a playful, slightly naughty way.
examples: The boy grinned *impishly* and ran off with the cookie.
She winked *impishly* at her sister.
“Maybe I did, maybe I didn't,” he said *impishly*.

position: before its word — before adjectives (*implausibly cheap*); front or mid as a comment

senses.gloss: In a way that is hard to believe.
examples: The apartment was *implausibly* cheap for Manhattan.
*Implausibly*, the hero survives the fall without a scratch.
The team *implausibly* came back from twenty points down.

position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it; end after *trust*, *believe*
comparison: more/most — in the first sense only
contrast: *implicitly* is the opposite of *explicitly* (прямо, открыто), but *trust someone implicitly* means trust them completely, not trust them indirectly.

senses.gloss: Without being said directly; understood from what is said or done.
examples: By not objecting, he *implicitly* agreed to the plan.
The contract *implicitly* allows the data to be shared.
The ad suggests, *implicitly*, that the car will make you happier.

senses.gloss: Completely, without any doubt; with *trust* or *believe*.
examples: I trust her *implicitly*.
The soldiers obeyed their commander *implicitly*.

position: end — usually after a verb of speaking or looking

senses.gloss: In a way that begs for something.
examples: The dog looked up at me *imploringly*.
“Please don't go,” she said *imploringly*.
He held out his hands *imploringly*.

position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it

senses.gloss: In a rude way; without good manners.
examples: He *impolitely* interrupted the speaker twice.
I'm sorry if I answered you *impolitely*.
She kept staring *impolitely* at his tattoos.

type: stance — marking the key point; also manner
position: front — in *more importantly*, *most importantly*, with a comma; end in the manner sense
modifies: clauses; verbs in the manner sense

senses.gloss: Used to point out the most significant fact, usually as *more importantly* or *most importantly*.
examples: The car is cheap and, *more importantly*, safe.
*Most importantly*, don't forget your passport.
*Importantly*, the study included both men and women.

senses.gloss: In a self-important way, as if you matter a lot.
examples: He walked *importantly* up to the podium.
The new manager strutted *importantly* around the office.

position: before its word

senses.gloss: Extremely; to a degree that seems impossible.
examples: The models all looked *impossibly* thin.
The deadline is *impossibly* tight.
She stayed *impossibly* calm during the crisis.

position: end — after the verb and its object

senses.gloss: Not exactly or accurately.
examples: The term is often used *imprecisely*.
The distance was measured *imprecisely*, so we had to redo it.
He described the location only *imprecisely*.

position: end — after the verb; before its word with adjectives (*impressively large*)

senses.gloss: In a way that makes people admire it.
examples: The team played *impressively* in the second half.
The museum's collection is *impressively* large.
She speaks four languages *impressively* well.

position: front — with a comma; also mid, and before its word with adjectives

senses.gloss: In a way that is surprising because it was not likely.
examples: *Improbably*, the smallest team won the championship.
The book is *improbably* funny for a book about taxes.
The old car *improbably* made it across the desert.

position: end — after the verb and its object; before participles (*improperly installed*)

senses.gloss: In a wrong or unacceptable way.
examples: The car seat was *improperly* installed.
Food that is stored *improperly* can make you sick.
Two officials were accused of acting *improperly*.

position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it

senses.gloss: Suddenly, without planning or thinking first.
examples: I *impulsively* bought a plane ticket to Paris.
Don't act *impulsively* when you're angry.
She shops *more impulsively* when she's stressed.

position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it

senses.gloss: Not correctly or exactly.
examples: The article *inaccurately* reported the number of victims.
His name was spelled *inaccurately* on the list.
The old map shows the border *inaccurately*.

position: before its word — before participles (*inadequately trained*); also end

senses.gloss: Not well enough, or not enough.
examples: Many of the new workers were *inadequately* trained.
The house was *inadequately* heated in winter.
The problem has been addressed *inadequately* so far.

position: mid — before the main verb; also end

senses.gloss: By accident, without meaning to.
examples: I *inadvertently* deleted the whole file.
He *inadvertently* left the back door unlocked.
The email was sent *inadvertently* to the entire company.

position: end — after the verb and its object

senses.gloss: In a silly, pointless way.
examples: He grinned *inanely* at the camera.
They chatted *inanely* about the weather for an hour.
The host laughed *inanely* at his own jokes.

position: end — after the verb and its object; before participles (*inappropriately dressed*)

senses.gloss: In a way that is not suitable or acceptable.
examples: He was fired for behaving *inappropriately* with clients.
She was *inappropriately* dressed for a funeral.
The teacher laughed *inappropriately* at the student's mistake.

position: end — usually after a verb of speaking or looking

senses.gloss: Too quietly to be heard.
examples: He muttered something *inaudibly* and left.
She whispered *inaudibly* to her friend.
The engine was running almost *inaudibly*.

position: end — usually after *begin*, *start*, *open*

senses.gloss: In a way that suggests things will not go well.
examples: The season began *inauspiciously* with three straight losses.
Their marriage started *inauspiciously*, in a snowstorm that closed the roads.
The new restaurant opened *inauspiciously* on the day of a blackout.

type: manner — without stopping, usually of something annoying
position: end — after the verb and its object

senses.gloss: Without stopping, again and again.
examples: The neighbor's dog barked *incessantly* all night.
It rained *incessantly* for a week.
He talks *incessantly* about his new car.

position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it

senses.gloss: In a clear, sharp way that goes straight to the point.
examples: She writes *incisively* about politics.
The report *incisively* identifies the company's weaknesses.
He argued *more incisively* than any other lawyer in the room.

position: end — after *travel*, *go*, *stay*
form: borrowed from Italian; the same form is an adjective
contrast: Also an adjective with the same meaning (*The star was incognito*); *incognito mode* in a web browser is the adjective.

senses.gloss: Hiding who you really are, especially when you are famous.
examples: The singer traveled *incognito* in a baseball cap and sunglasses.
The CEO went *incognito* to see how the stores were really run.
The prince spent a week in New York *incognito*.

position: end — after the verb and its object

senses.gloss: In a confused way that is hard to understand.
examples: The man was mumbling *incoherently* when the police arrived.
She was so upset that she spoke *incoherently*.
The report was written *incoherently*, jumping from topic to topic.

position: before its word — before adjectives and comparatives (*incomparably better*)

senses.gloss: Far more than anything else; beyond comparison.
examples: The new phone is *incomparably* faster than the old one.
She was an *incomparably* gifted pianist.
Life in the city is *incomparably* more expensive.

position: end — after the verb and its object

senses.gloss: Without the skill or ability to do something well.
examples: The project was managed *incompetently* from the start.
The repairs were done so *incompetently* that we had to redo them.
Critics say the city handled the snowstorm *incompetently*.

position: end — after the verb and its object; before participles (*incompletely understood*)

senses.gloss: Not fully; with parts missing.
examples: The process is still *incompletely* understood.
The form was filled out *incompletely*, so it was rejected.
The old wound had healed only *incompletely*.

position: before its word

senses.gloss: To a degree that is almost impossible to imagine.
examples: The universe is *inconceivably* large.
The price was *inconceivably* high for a used car.
Ten years ago, this technology would have seemed *inconceivably* advanced.

position: end — usually after *end*, *close*, *finish*

senses.gloss: Without a clear result or decision.
examples: The peace talks ended *inconclusively* late last night.
The investigation closed *inconclusively*, with no one charged.
The debate ended *inconclusively*, with neither side giving ground.

position: end — after the verb; also before its word (*incongruously cheerful*)

senses.gloss: In a way that seems strange or out of place.
examples: A pink plastic flamingo stood *incongruously* in the snowy yard.
The music was *incongruously* cheerful for such a sad movie.
He was dressed *incongruously* in a tuxedo at the barbecue.

position: end — after the verb and its object

senses.gloss: Not in the same way every time.
examples: The rules are enforced *inconsistently* from school to school.
The team has played *inconsistently* all season.
The word is spelled *inconsistently* throughout the report.

position: end — after the verb and its object

senses.gloss: Without attracting attention.
examples: I slipped out of the meeting as *inconspicuously* as possible.
The camera was mounted *inconspicuously* above the door.
The detective sat *inconspicuously* in the corner of the diner.

position: before its word — before participles (*inconveniently located*); also end, or front with a comma

senses.gloss: In a way that causes trouble or comes at a bad time.
examples: The only pharmacy is *inconveniently* located on the other side of town.
The meeting was *inconveniently* scheduled for 7 a.m.
*Inconveniently*, my phone died just as the taxi arrived.

position: end — after the verb and its object; before participles (*incorrectly labeled*)

senses.gloss: In a way that is wrong or not true.
examples: You answered the last question *incorrectly*.
The box was *incorrectly* labeled as fragile.
Many people pronounce the word *incorrectly*.

position: before its word — before adjectives (*increasingly difficult*); mid before verbs; front with a comma
contrast: *increasingly* already means 'more and more', so *increasingly more difficult* is redundant: say *increasingly difficult* or *more and more difficult* (всё труднее).

senses.gloss: More and more, over time.
examples: It's becoming *increasingly* difficult to find a cheap apartment.
*Increasingly*, people are choosing to work from home.
She grew *increasingly* worried as the hours passed.

position: end — usually after a verb of speaking or looking

senses.gloss: In a way that shows you cannot believe something.
examples: “You won the lottery?” she asked *incredulously*.
He stared *incredulously* at the bill.
The crowd watched *incredulously* as the underdog took the lead.

position: before its word — before adjectives (*incurably ill*, *incurably romantic*)

senses.gloss: In a way that cannot be cured or changed.
examples: By the time the doctors found the tumor, he was *incurably* ill.
She's an *incurably* romantic person.
My father is *incurably* optimistic about his baseball team.

position: end — after the verb; before its word with adjectives (*indecently early*)

senses.gloss: In a shocking or improper way; more than is acceptable.
examples: He was arrested for exposing himself *indecently* in the park.
Her skirt was *indecently* short for a job interview.
We left the party *indecently* early.

position: end — after the verb and its object

senses.gloss: Unable to decide; in a hesitant way.
examples: She hovered *indecisively* between the two dresses.
The mayor has acted *indecisively* throughout the crisis.
He stood *indecisively* at the door, not sure whether to knock.

position: before its word — before participles (*indelibly printed*); also end

senses.gloss: Permanently, in a way that cannot be removed or forgotten.
examples: That summer is *indelibly* printed on my memory.
The war marked his generation *indelibly*.
The name was written *indelibly* on the label with a marker.

position: end — after the verb and its object; *independently of* before a noun
contrast: Russian *независимо от* is usually *regardless of*: *regardless of the weather*, not *independently of the weather*. *Independently of* (not *from*) means separately from: *The two systems work independently of each other*.

senses.gloss: On your own, without help or control from others.
examples: The kids learned to work *independently* at a young age.
She lives *independently* despite her disability.
The investigation will be run *independently* of the police department.

senses.gloss: Separately, without any contact or influence between the people or things involved.
examples: Two scientists discovered the same process *independently*.
Each witness was interviewed *independently*.

position: before its word

senses.gloss: To a degree too great to describe.
examples: The view from the top was *indescribably* beautiful.
The smell in the room was *indescribably* bad.
I felt *indescribably* happy when I saw her again.

position: end — usually after a verb of speaking or looking

senses.gloss: Without interest or concern.
examples: He shrugged *indifferently* when I told him the news.
The clerk glanced *indifferently* at my ticket and waved me through.
The staff treated our complaints *indifferently*.

position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it

senses.gloss: In an angry way, because something seems unfair.
examples: “I did not take your pen!” he said *indignantly*.
She *indignantly* denied the rumor.
Customers complained *indignantly* about the price increase.

position: end — after the verb and its object; before participles (*indirectly caused*)

senses.gloss: Not directly; through another person, thing or step.
examples: The new law will affect everyone, directly or *indirectly*.
She hinted *indirectly* that she wanted to leave.
The fire was *indirectly* caused by the heat wave.

position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it
contrast: *indiscreetly* = without keeping secrets (неосторожно, болтливо); *indiscriminately* = without choosing (без разбора).

senses.gloss: Carelessly, saying or showing things that should stay private.
examples: He *indiscreetly* mentioned the surprise party in front of her.
The details of the deal were *indiscreetly* leaked to the press.
She talked *indiscreetly* about her boss at the bar.

position: end — after the verb and its object

senses.gloss: Without choosing carefully; at random.
examples: The gunman fired *indiscriminately* into the crowd.
Antibiotics should not be used *indiscriminately*.
He reads *indiscriminately*, from comic books to philosophy.

position: end — after the verb and its object

senses.gloss: Not clearly enough to be seen, heard or remembered well.
examples: He spoke so *indistinctly* that nobody understood him.
Through the fog we could see the lighthouse only *indistinctly*.
Voices murmured *indistinctly* behind the wall.

position: end — after the verb and its object; before participles (*individually wrapped*); front with a comma

senses.gloss: Separately, one at a time.
examples: The candies are *individually* wrapped.
The teacher met with each student *individually*.
*Individually*, the players are good, but they don't work well as a team.

position: end — usually after a verb of speaking or looking
contrast: Russian *снисходительно* has two English matches: *indulgently* is warm and tolerant; *condescendingly* is the negative one, looking down on someone.

senses.gloss: In a kind, tolerant way, letting someone have what they want.
examples: Grandma smiled *indulgently* as the kids ate their third dessert.
The teacher listened *indulgently* to his long excuse.
Her parents treated her *indulgently* and rarely said no.

position: end — after the verb and its object
contrast: *industriously* is about working hard (усердно), not about industry; 'by industry' is *industrially*.

senses.gloss: In a hard-working, busy way.
examples: The students worked *industriously* on their projects.
Ants moved *industriously* back and forth across the path.
She typed away *industriously* all afternoon.

position: end — after the verb and its object

senses.gloss: Without producing the result you want.
examples: The problem has been handled *ineffectively* for years.
He tried *ineffectively* to calm the angry crowd.
Money that is spent *ineffectively* doesn't help anyone.

position: end — after the verb and its object

senses.gloss: In a weak way that fails to achieve anything.
examples: She waved her arms *ineffectually* at the swarm of bees.
The police tried *ineffectually* to stop the protest.
He pushed *ineffectually* against the heavy door.

position: end — after the verb and its object
contrast: Russian *неэффективно* covers two words: *ineffectively* = without getting the result; *inefficiently* = wasting time, money or energy along the way.

senses.gloss: In a way that wastes time, money or energy.
examples: Old buildings use energy very *inefficiently*.
The office is run *inefficiently*, with far too many meetings.
The factory was operating *inefficiently* before the upgrade.

position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it

senses.gloss: Without skill; clumsily.
examples: The new manager handled the crisis *ineptly*.
He *ineptly* tried to fix the sink and flooded the kitchen.
The movie is *ineptly* edited and hard to follow.

position: before its word — before adjectives and participles (*inescapably clear*); also front

senses.gloss: In a way that cannot be avoided or denied.
examples: The conclusion is *inescapably* clear: we need more money.
*Inescapably*, the costs will be passed on to customers.
Her life is *inescapably* tied to the town where she grew up.

position: front — with a comma; also mid, before the main verb

senses.gloss: As was certain to happen; unavoidably.
examples: *Inevitably*, the project cost more than planned.
Prices will *inevitably* go up next year.
Whenever we talk politics, it *inevitably* ends in an argument.

position: before its word — before adjectives (*inexcusably late*); also end

senses.gloss: In a way that is too bad to be forgiven.
examples: The train was *inexcusably* late again.
He behaved *inexcusably* toward his sister.
The report was *inexcusably* careless with the numbers.

position: mid or end — before the main verb or after it

senses.gloss: In a way that cannot be stopped or changed.
examples: Prices have risen slowly but *inexorably*.
The river is *inexorably* eating away at the cliff.
The country moved *inexorably* toward war.

position: end — after the verb and its object; before participles (*inexpensively priced*)

senses.gloss: Without costing much money.
examples: You can furnish an apartment *inexpensively* with used furniture.
The hotel is *inexpensively* priced but very clean.
We ate *inexpensively* at food trucks during the trip.

position: before its word — before participles (*inextricably linked*)

senses.gloss: So closely that the things cannot be separated.
examples: Poverty and poor health are *inextricably* linked.
His name is *inextricably* tied to the company he founded.
The two stories are *inextricably* bound together.

position: end — after *laugh*, *smile*; before its word with adjectives (*infectiously cheerful*)

senses.gloss: In a way that quickly spreads the feeling to other people.
examples: She laughed *infectiously*, and soon the whole room was laughing.
The song is *infectiously* catchy.
He's *infectiously* enthusiastic about everything he does.

position: before its word — before comparatives and adjectives (*infinitely better*)

senses.gloss: Very much; far, usually before a comparative.
examples: This version is *infinitely* better than the first one.
I'd *infinitely* prefer to stay home tonight.

senses.gloss: Without any limit or end.
examples: In theory, the line can be extended *infinitely* in both directions.
The pattern on the screen seemed to repeat *infinitely*.
